newsitem.title: ITALY: Lira, BTP not overshooting, valued prudently - BOI.
newsitem.headline: Lira, BTP not overshooting, valued prudently - BOI.

text.p: The recent appreciation of the Italian lira and government bonds on the financial markets does not represent "overshooting" but a realistic valuation of Italy's economic efforts, a senior Bank of Italy official said.

Tommaso Padoa-Schioppa, vice director general of the Bank of Italy, said in a speech released ahead of delivery to foreign bankers here that on the contrary, markets were still evaluating Italy with understandable caution.

"The virtuous circle begun in the last six months of inflation, interest rates, the exchange rate and public spending is not unjustified euphoria of traders in search of easy capital gains but a realistic evaluation of the progress already made," Padoa-Schioppa said.
"The improvement in prices on state securities and the lira, while fast and significant, does not present the characteristics of overshooting," he said.
"I would say on the contrary the market is showing an understandable prudence, demonstrated by a differential with countries like Spain and Sweden which is to our disadvantage."

But he added that despite progress so far to achieve macroeconomic equilibrium, much remained to do to make a lasting correction to the imbalance in public finances, reduce unemployment and create lasting price stability.

Padoa-Schioppa said the lira's parity in Europe's exchange rate mechanism, which is 990 per mark, was consistent with the aim of consolidating results achieved on inflation, maintaining competitive costs and prices in European and world markets.
"Temporary exchange rate movements from the reference value will be tolerated to keep alive the perception that the market can move in both directions (two-way risk)," he said.
"But the force drawing the exchange rate back to a line of stability will be the maintenance of price stability," he said.
History had shown the economy grew and created jobs in a lasting way only if prices were stable and public finances were in order, he said.

Employment growth was possible if there was consistent behaviour from the monetary authority to fight inflation, by the government in cleaning up finances, and by unions and industry on wage demands and on pricing policy.

The Bank of Italy was working hard to make ordinary Italian consumers, employers and unions understand that the normal inflation rate should be around two percent and that when it was at four percent prices had to slow down significantly.
"This means a real change in the order of priorities, a change in the mental parameters without which you cannot say you have achieved a return to price stability," he said.
